gloss: Hōjōki; An Account of My Hut (1212 essay)

definitions.explanation: A short essay written in 1212 by {鴨長明|かものちょうめい}. After describing the fires, whirlwind, famine, and earthquake that struck Kyoto, the author tells of retiring to a tiny hut about three meters square (a {方丈|ほうじょう}) to live simply. It is the classic statement of impermanence in Japanese prose.

examples.english: Hōjōki was written by Kamo no Chōmei.

examples.japanese: ⟦{大|おお}きな→大きな：02849_ookina⟧⟦{地震|じしん}→地震：01608_jishin⟧のあとで、{方丈記|ほうじょうき}⟦を→を：00422_wo⟧⟦{読|よ}み{直|なお}す→読み直す：29840_yominaosu⟧⟦{人|ひと}→人：00476_hito⟧⟦が→が：00051_ga⟧⟦{増|ふ}えた→増える：01183_fueru⟧そうだ。
examples.english: I hear that after the big earthquake, more people went back to reading Hōjōki.

notes:
The opening compares human life and dwellings to the water of a river and to bubbles, and is quoted whenever people reflect on how quickly things change.

COMMON EXPRESSIONS:
- {行|ゆ}く⟦{川|かわ}→川：02186_kawa⟧⟦の→の：09472_no⟧⟦{流|なが}れ→流れ：03504_nagare⟧⟦は→は：00079_ha⟧⟦{絶|た}えず→絶えず：15260_taezu⟧して、しかももとの⟦{水|みず}→水：02258_mizu⟧にあらず: "The flowing river never stops, and yet the water is never the same" — the opening line
- よどみに⟦{浮|う}かぶ→浮かぶ：03916_ukabu⟧うたかた: foam floating on still water — the image of fleeting life
- {方丈|ほうじょう}: a room ten feet square; also the abbot's quarters in a Zen temple

CULTURAL NOTE:
Because it records real disasters in plain detail, Hōjōki is also read as early disaster literature, and interest in it rose again after the 2011 earthquake.
